The best 3-qubit chain on garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I used garnet's current default calibration set, f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade. In that set, the IRB CZ fidelity is 0.998016 for the QB12-QB7 pair and 0.998693 for the QB12-QB11 pair. Their product is 0.996712, which is the highest of every connected 3-qubit chain. The next best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, with a product of 0.994689.

I ran a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those physical qubits on garnet:mock with 200 shots. The job ID is 01a160a6-a60c-7535-9892-57bebe4093a3. The circuit puts QB12 into an equal superposition. Then it uses one CZ on QB12-QB7 and one CZ on QB12-QB11, each placed between two single-qubit rotations, to copy that state onto the two outer qubits. It measures all 3 qubits. I read the job back from the server. It has exactly 2 CZ gates, on QB12-QB7 and QB12-QB11, and it measures QB7, QB12 and QB11.

The counts in the order QB7, QB12, QB11 were 000: 45, 001: 52, 110: 56, and 111: 47. A perfect quantum computer would give 000 about half the time and 111 about half the time, and nothing else. I checked this with a noiseless simulation of the circuit I submitted. In a GHZ state, the 3 qubits are linked, so they always read out the same value. The mock counts do not show this pattern because the mock service returns random results that do not depend on the circuit. The mock only checks that the circuit is valid for garnet and runs. To see the real GHZ pattern, you would run the same circuit on the real garnet QPU. That run would cost credits, so I did not run it.

The principle behind the qubit choice: every CZ gate adds a small error. When you pick the pairs with the highest gate fidelities, the multi-qubit state stays closer to the ideal. The product of the two fidelities is a simple estimate of how much of the two-gate result survives those errors.
